explanations.explanation: Jesus says it Himself: "…My Father is the keeper of the vineyard." So the vine is Jesus and the keeper of the whole vineyard is His Father. Then Jesus says what the keeper does: He cuts off every branch that bears no fruit and prunes every branch that does bear fruit.
John the Baptist was the man who pointed people to Jesus (John 1:29), so I see why his name came up. But Jesus never mentions him in this picture. He names the keeper right away, and it's His Father.
Isaiah is a big name to reach for, and I see why you did. But Jesus doesn't bring him up here. He says, "…My Father is the keeper of the vineyard." The Father is the one named as keeper.

I get the thought. A branch already making fruit sounds like it should be left alone. But Jesus says the keeper prunes every branch that does bear fruit. He does it "…to make it even more fruitful." So the fruitful branches get attention too.

The keeper does not leave them alone. Jesus says, "…every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful." Fruit is not where the keeper stops. He keeps working on those branches so they bear more.
That's the word. The keeper prunes the branches that bear fruit "…to make it even more fruitful." The pruning has a goal, and the goal is more fruit. Nobody's just trimming for fun.
Colorful would make a pretty vine, and I do love a rainbow. But Jesus doesn't say a word about color. He says the keeper prunes the fruit-bearing branches to make them even more fruitful.
Sturdy sounds like a good reason to trim a branch. But that's not the word Jesus uses. He says the keeper prunes them "…to make it even more fruitful." so the aim is fruit.

explanations.answer: The word He has spoken to them
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you." The cause He names is His word. He says "already," so He's describing where they are right now.

explanations.answer: The fast they kept this week
explanations.explanation: A fast is a serious thing to do. But Jesus never mentions one here. He says they're clean "…because of the word I have spoken to you."

explanations.answer: The sacrifice they brought to the temple
explanations.explanation: A sacrifice is a serious thing to bring, so I see why that came to mind. But Jesus doesn't point to one here. He says, "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you."

Jesus says the opposite. "Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me." Picture a branch lying on the ground trying to make fruit. That branch is not producing anything.

Right, a branch can't do it alone. Jesus says, "Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me." The fruit comes from staying connected to the vine.

explanations.answer: It is thrown away and burned
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says. Anyone who doesn't remain in Him "…is like a branch that is thrown away and withers." Then He says, "Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned." It's a serious picture, and Jesus says it plainly.
Grafting is a real thing gardeners do, so it's a fair guess. But Jesus doesn't say it here. He says the branch is thrown away and withers, then gathered up and burned.

explanations.answer: It is pruned to grow again
explanations.explanation: Pruning is in this passage, but it's for a different branch. In verse 2 the keeper prunes the branches that bear fruit, to make them more fruitful. The branch that doesn't remain in Jesus is thrown away, withers and is burned (John 15:6).

That's what Jesus says: "If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you." Notice it starts with "if." The asking is tied to remaining in Him and His words remaining in them.

This one is true. Jesus says, "If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you." The "if" matters, because it's tied to remaining in Him and His words staying in them.

That's it. Jesus says it's to His Father's glory "…that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples." The fruit shows who they belong to. So the same fruit that proves they're His disciples is to His Father's glory.

explanations.answer: That they have earned a reward
explanations.explanation: Reward is a natural thing to guess. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says bearing much fruit is "…proving yourselves to be My disciples."

explanations.answer: That they will never be tested
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't promise that in this passage. What He says is that bearing much fruit is "…proving yourselves to be My disciples." The fruit shows who they belong to, and nothing in these verses says they'll skip hard things.
Jesus says, "As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love." He gives them a place to stay, and it's His love. After all that vine talk, He's still saying remain.
Jesus does say remain here, so the verb is right. But He doesn't point them to a city. He says, "Remain in My love."
Same verb, different address. Jesus doesn't send them to a building. He says, "As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love."
That's the word. Jesus says, "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love…" He also points to His own example. He kept His Father's commandments and remains in His love.

Promises are a good thing, but Jesus uses a different word. He says, "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love…" The word He picks is commandments, and what comes with keeping them is remaining in His love.
Traditions are not the word Jesus uses here. He says, "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love…" He keeps it simple, which I respect.

Jesus says it Himself: "…just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love." He is not asking them to do something He hasn't done. He says it right in the middle of talking about the disciples remaining in His love.

This one is true. First Jesus says, "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love…" Then He adds, "…just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love." So He has kept His Father's commandments and remains in His love.

explanations.answer: So His joy may be in them and theirs be complete
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete." The reason is joy. He wants His joy in them, and wants theirs to be full.

explanations.answer: So they will not be afraid of the crowds again
explanations.explanation: That's a believable reason. But the text doesn't give it. Jesus says He has told them these things "…so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete."

explanations.answer: So they can teach in the synagogues tomorrow
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't mention teaching in synagogues here. He says why He's talking: "…so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete." The reason is joy.

explanations.answer: Love one another as He has loved them
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you." The measure is how He has loved them. That's the whole command.

explanations.answer: Pray for one another every day and night
explanations.explanation: Praying for each other is a good thing, but Jesus doesn't give that as His commandment here. He says, "…that you love one another as I have loved you." He says it again in verse 17: "This is My command to you: Love one another."

explanations.answer: Forgive one another whenever they are wronged
explanations.explanation: Forgiving one another is a good thing, but Jesus doesn't give it as His commandment here. He says, "…that you love one another as I have loved you." He says it again in verse 17: "This is My command to you: Love one another."

explanations.answer: Laying down his life for his friends
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends." That's a heavy thing to say, and He says it plainly. I think it's one to sit with for a second.
Giving away everything would be generous. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says, "Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends."

Forgiving someone is big, and Jesus talks about it in another place (Matthew 18:21-22). But that's not what He names here. He says, "Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends."
Jesus says, "You are My friends if you do what I command you." He's telling them who His friends are. And what He commands is what He's been saying: love one another.
This one is true. Jesus says, "You are My friends if you do what I command you." So friendship with Him is tied to doing what He commands.
That's the word. Jesus says, "…a servant does not understand what his master is doing." Then He tells the disciples, "No longer do I call you servants…" So He's not treating them as servants.

Jesus isn't talking about a neighbor here. He's talking about a servant and his master: "…a servant does not understand what his master is doing." Then He tells the disciples, "No longer do I call you servants…"
Jesus isn't comparing a servant to a brother. He's talking about a servant and his master: "…a servant does not understand what his master is doing." Then He says, "But I have called you friends…"

Jesus says, "…I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you." The reason is that He's told them everything He learned from His Father. That's why He says He no longer calls them servants.
This one is true. Jesus says, "…I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you." That's His reason for calling them friends.
Close, but Jesus turns it the other way. He says, "You did not choose Me, but I chose you." So the text says the disciples did not choose Him. Choosing Him first isn't what Jesus says.
Right, it's the other way around. Jesus says, "You did not choose Me, but I chose you." He did the choosing.
Jesus says, "…I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain…" So it's fruit, and it's the kind that remains. That takes us right back to the vine and the branches.

Building a great house is a big project, but Jesus doesn't give it to them here. He says, "…I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain…" The job He names is fruit, and He says it's fruit that will remain.

Gate guard sounds like a job with a whistle and a clipboard, and with this mustache in the way I'd be terrible at it. But Jesus doesn't appoint them to that. He says, "…I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain…" That's the assignment.
Jesus says, "…whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you." The asking goes to the Father, and it's in Jesus' name. He gives them the way to ask.
Moses is a big name, so I see why it came to mind. But Jesus doesn't say to ask in his name. He says to ask the Father "…in My name…"
Abraham is a giant name in Israel's story, so that's a natural guess. But Jesus doesn't point to him here. He says, "…whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you."
